title: Predator hunting strategies
keyIdea: Predators have different ways to catch their prey. Wolves hunt together in a pack, so they can catch animals much bigger than one wolf. A chameleon shoots out a long sticky tongue. Many spiders build a web trap. A crocodile hides in the water and waits for prey to come close, then strikes. Prey animals have defences too: spines and armour, a bad smell or poison, and tricks such as playing dead. Over many generations, faster prey and faster predators survive, so both keep getting better: this is called an arms race.
familyTip: Watch a nature clip together, or a spider's web in the garden. Ask two questions: how does this hunter catch its food, and how does its prey try to stay safe? Sort what you see into chase, team, trap or ambush, and spines, poison, smell or trick.

visual.caption: Is it a hunter's trick or a prey animal's defence? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match hunters to their tricks, time a crocodile ambush, corner a moose with a wolf pack, sort prey defences and run an arms race.

kid: A predator hunts other animals for food. The animal it hunts is its prey. Wolves hunt as a team, called a pack. Together they can catch a moose that is far bigger than one wolf.

A chameleon sits still and shoots out a long sticky tongue to grab a fly. Many spiders build a sticky web and wait. A crocodile hides in the river with just its eyes showing. When an animal comes close to drink, it strikes. This is called an ambush.
Prey fight back. A porcupine has sharp quills. A skunk sprays a bad smell. A poison dart frog is bright, to warn that it is poisonous. An opossum plays dead.
Over a very long time, the fast prey get away and have babies that are fast too. So the prey get faster, and only fast hunters catch enough food. This is an arms race.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This builds on food chains and habitats in the National Curriculum in England (Years 2 to 4: living things, food chains, predators and prey) and NGSS 3-LS4-3 and 4-LS1-1 (structures and behaviours that help animals survive). It looks ahead to Year 6 evolution and inheritance through the idea of an arms race.

The facts in the lab: grey wolves hunt large prey such as elk and moose cooperatively, testing, chasing and cornering them. Chameleons catch insects with a ballistic, sticky-tipped tongue that can reach more than their body length. Many, but not all, spiders build webs. Crocodiles are ambush predators that wait at the water's edge. Porcupine quills, armadillo plates, skunk spray, poison dart frog toxins with warning colours, and playing dead (thanatosis) are well-documented defences. Zebra stripes are often said to confuse lions, but the strongest evidence now is that they deter biting flies, so the lab does not use them.

Common mistakes: thinking animals choose or try to change their bodies, or that practice is passed on to their young; the arms race step shows that the slowest prey are caught and the rest pass on their speed. Children also think bright colours are for hiding, that every predator chases its prey, and that a hunt is just luck. The ambush and pack steps show that waiting and teamwork are strategies, not laziness.

practice.prompt: How does a crocodile usually catch its prey?
choices: It hides in the water and strikes when prey comes close
It chases prey a long way across the grass
practice.hint: Think about where a crocodile lies, and what it waits for.
practice.explain: A crocodile is an ambush hunter. It hides in the water and strikes when an animal comes close to drink.

practice.prompt: A pack has {w} wolves. {y} of them are young and stay at the den. How many wolves go on the hunt?
practice.hint: Start with the whole pack and take away the young ones who stay behind.
practice.explain: {w} take away {y} is {=w-y}, so {=w-y} wolves hunt together as a team.

practice.prompt: A herd has {g} gazelles. A cheetah catches the {c} slowest ones over a month. How many gazelles are left to have young?
practice.hint: Take the caught gazelles away from the whole herd.
practice.explain: {g} − {c} = {=g-c}. The ones left are the faster gazelles, so their young are likely to be fast too.

practice.prompt: Why is a poison dart frog brightly coloured?
choices: To warn predators that it is poisonous
practice.hint: Do bright colours help an animal hide, or stand out?
practice.explain: Bright colours stand out. They warn predators: I am poisonous, so do not eat me.

practice.prompt: How does an opossum try to stay safe?
practice.hint: It does not fight or run. It does something surprising instead.
practice.explain: An opossum lies still and plays dead. Many predators lose interest in prey that does not move.

pool.prompt: Why do wolves hunt in a pack?
choices: So they can catch prey much bigger than one wolf
So they can build a web
pool.hint: Could one wolf catch a moose on its own?
pool.explain: Working as a team, wolves can chase and corner big animals like moose that one wolf could not catch.

pool.prompt: How does a chameleon catch a fly?
choices: It shoots out a long sticky tongue
It chases the fly through the air
pool.hint: A chameleon moves slowly, but one part of it is very fast.
pool.explain: A chameleon sits still and shoots out its long sticky tongue to grab the fly.

pool.prompt: A spider's web catches {f} flies in the morning and {a} more in the afternoon. How many flies does it catch in all?
pool.hint: Add the morning flies and the afternoon flies.
pool.explain: {f} + {a} = {=f+a} flies. The spider waits while its web trap does the work.

pool.prompt: How does a skunk stay safe?
pool.hint: Think of the defence you could notice with your nose.
pool.explain: A skunk sprays a horrible smell, and predators learn to stay away from it.

pool.prompt: A crocodile strikes when a gnu is still far away. What happens?
choices: The gnu sees it and runs away
pool.hint: An ambush works best when the prey has no time to run.
pool.explain: Striking too soon gives the gnu time to run. An ambush hunter waits until prey is very close.

pool.prompt: Which gazelle is most likely to be caught by a cheetah?
pool.hint: Which gazelle has the least chance to get away?
pool.explain: The slowest gazelle is the easiest to catch. The fast ones are more likely to escape.

pool.prompt: Over many years, gazelles have become faster. Why?
choices: Fast gazelles survived more often and had fast young
Each gazelle chose to grow faster legs
They practised running and passed it on
pool.hint: Can an animal choose its body, or pass on practice?
pool.explain: Slow gazelles were caught more often. The fast ones lived to have young that were fast like them.

pool.prompt: A porcupine has about {k} thousand quills. A predator pulls out {p} thousand of them. About how many thousand are left?
pool.hint: Take the lost quills away from the starting number. Both numbers are in thousands.
pool.explain: {k} − {p} = {=k-p} thousand quills are left, still plenty to keep the porcupine safe. Lost quills grow back.
